title: (Scenario) You provisioned a VPC/subnet CIDR but ran out of IP addresses — why can't you simply resize a subnet CIDR in place, and how do you expand capacity without disrupting workloads (associate an ADDITIONAL (secondary) CIDR block to the VPC, create new subnets from it, then migrate/scale workloads into them gradually)?
shortTitle: Scenario — Ran Out of IP Addresses; Expanding with a Secondary CIDR

s1_definition.profdef: A subnet's CIDR is fixed at creation and cannot be resized in place, because its address range is already allocated and in use, and changing it would renumber live interfaces. To add capacity you associate an additional secondary CIDR block with the VPC, create new subnets from that block, and migrate or scale workloads into the new subnets gradually, draining the old ones without downtime.
s1_definition.analogy: A subnet is like a floor at National Bank of India with a fixed set of room numbers, say 101 to 150, and staff are already sitting in those rooms. You cannot simply declare the floor now runs 101 to 300, because the walls are built and people are working — renumbering would force everyone to move at once and chaos follows. Instead you lease a whole new floor (a secondary CIDR), build new rooms there, and move teams over one at a time while the old floor keeps working, until the old floor is empty.
s1_definition.oneliner: You cannot grow a subnet in place because its range is fixed and in use; you add a secondary CIDR to the VPC, build new subnets, and migrate workloads into them gradually.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A subnet's CIDR is fixed at creation and cannot be resized in place, because its address range is already allocated and in use, and changing it would renumber live interfaces. To add capacity you associate an additional secondary CIDR block with the VPC, create new subnets from that block, and migrate or scale workloads into the new subnets gradually, draining the old ones without downtime.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A subnet is like a floor at National Bank of India with a fixed set of room numbers, say 101 to 150, and staff are already sitting in those rooms. You cannot simply declare the floor now runs 101 to 300, because the walls are built and people are working — renumbering would force everyone to move at once and chaos follows. Instead you lease a whole new floor (a secondary CIDR), build new rooms there, and move teams over one at a time while the old floor keeps working, until the old floor is empty.

**One line to remember:** You cannot grow a subnet in place because its range is fixed and in use; you add a secondary CIDR to the VPC, build new subnets, and migrate workloads into them gradually.

sections.s2_technical:
A subnet CIDR is immutable. When you create a /24 subnet you get 251 usable addresses, and AWS allocates that range to the subnet. Resources attach elastic network interfaces with IPs from it. You cannot expand it to a /23 later because the adjacent address space may already belong to another subnet, and even if it did not, resizing would require renumbering interfaces that are actively serving traffic. So AWS simply does not allow it.

The supported path is to add capacity at the VPC level. You associate a secondary CIDR block with the existing VPC — the VPC can hold several CIDR blocks. From that new block you create new, larger subnets in each Availability Zone. Then you move workloads into them in a controlled way.

```text
# VPC originally: 10.0.0.0/16, app subnets nearly full
# Associate a secondary CIDR:
aws ec2 associate-vpc-cidr-block --vpc-id vpc-0abc --cidr-block 100.64.0.0/16
# Create larger new subnets from it, e.g. 100.64.0.0/20 per AZ, then migrate.
```

Migration is gradual and non-disruptive. For an auto-scaling group you add the new subnets to its configuration and let new instances launch there, then scale down the old ones. For EKS you add the new subnets to the cluster so new pods get IPs from the roomy block. For a database you provision a replica or a new instance in the new subnet and fail over. At no point do you renumber a running interface; you drain the old and fill the new.

A senior nuance: a common trick for IP exhaustion caused by EKS pods is to associate a secondary CIDR from the 100.64.0.0/10 carrier-grade NAT range, keep your nodes in the original routable range, and put pods on the secondary range via the CNI's custom networking. This gives pods a huge private pool without consuming your scarce routable space, and it is a standard pattern when a bank's EKS cluster grows faster than the original plan anticipated. Also, any peered VPC or Transit Gateway must have routes updated for the new secondary CIDR, and it must still not overlap with anything it connects to.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The settlement EKS cluster grew and its subnets ran out of pod IPs, so new pods fail to start and deployments stall. The team's first instinct is to make the subnet bigger, which AWS forbids. This is exactly what a secondary CIDR plus new subnets solves.

Problem 2 — The expansion must not take the running settlement service down. This is exactly why we migrate gradually — add new subnets, launch new capacity there, drain the old.

We will build a `VpcCapacity` model that refuses in-place subnet resize, supports associating a secondary CIDR, creates new subnets, and tracks a gradual migration. Classes: `Subnet`, `Vpc`, `MigrationPlan`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a VPC 10.0.0.0/16 with an app subnet 10.0.1.0/24 that is fully exhausted at 251 addresses.

Step 1 — The old subnet is full. The team tries to resize it from a /24 to a /23 in place. The `Subnet.resize` method throws, because a subnet CIDR is immutable — the adjacent space may belong to another subnet and live interfaces cannot be renumbered. The log records that the in-place resize is blocked and states the correct approach.

Step 2 — A secondary CIDR 100.64.0.0/16 is associated with the VPC. A VPC can hold several CIDR blocks, so this adds address space without touching the primary range.

Step 3 — A new, larger subnet 100.64.0.0/20 is created from the secondary CIDR, giving about four thousand usable addresses — ample for the growing EKS pods.

Step 4 — The `MigrationPlan` moves workloads in batches: first 100, then the remaining 151. Each batch releases capacity on the old subnet and consumes it on the new one. Nothing is renumbered mid-flight; the old subnet drains while the new one fills, so the settlement service stays up throughout.

```
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [WARNING] In-place resize blocked: subnet CIDR is immutable — associate a secondary VPC CIDR and migrate instead
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Migration status: 251 workloads migrated; old remaining=251, new remaining=3840
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Old subnet 10.0.1.0/24 (FULL, 251 used)
    │ resize("/23")  ✗ UnsupportedOperation (immutable)
    ▼
  VPC associate secondary CIDR 100.64.0.0/16
    │
    ▼
  New subnet 100.64.0.0/20 (~4091 usable)
    │ migrate in batches (drain old → fill new)
    ├─ batch 100 ──→ old 151 left, new 100 used
    └─ batch 151 ──→ old empty,   new 251 used
    (no live interface renumbered → zero downtime)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Capacity + Migration ═══

  ┌─ Patterns ─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Immutable value: subnet CIDR fixed → resize throws       │
  │ Gradual migration: drain-and-fill, no renumber           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: Vpc manages CIDRs; MigrationPlan manages the move     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────┐ creates ┌──────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐
  │ Vpc      │────────→│ Subnet       │←──│ MigrationPlan  │
  │ + assoc  │         │ + resize()✗  │   │ + migrateBatch │
  │ Secondary│         │ + remaining()│   │ + status()     │
  └──────────┘         └──────────────┘   └────────────────┘

  Contract for resize(newCidr):
    Always throws UnsupportedOperationException (CIDR immutable)
  Contract for migrateBatch(n):
    Post: old.used -= n, new.used += n, no interface renumbered
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When a subnet runs out of IP addresses, the instinct is to make the subnet bigger, but AWS does not allow resizing a subnet CIDR in place, and there is a good reason. The subnet's range is fixed at creation and already in use — resources have elastic network interfaces with IPs from it, and the adjacent address space may belong to another subnet. Expanding it would mean renumbering live interfaces that are actively serving traffic, which is disruptive and ambiguous, so AWS simply makes the subnet CIDR immutable.

The supported way to add capacity is at the VPC level. A VPC can hold several CIDR blocks, so I associate an additional secondary CIDR with the existing VPC, then create new, larger subnets from that block in each Availability Zone. After that I migrate workloads into the new subnets gradually, which is the part that keeps it non-disruptive. I never renumber a running interface; I drain the old subnet and fill the new one.

How I migrate depends on the workload. For an auto-scaling group I add the new subnets to its configuration, let new instances launch in the roomy subnets, and scale the old ones down. For EKS I add the new subnets to the cluster so new pods get IPs from the big block. For a database I bring up a replica or a new instance in the new subnet and fail over. In every case capacity shifts gradually, so the settlement service stays up the whole time.

At National Bank of India this happened when our settlement EKS cluster grew faster than the original plan and pod IPs ran out, stalling deployments. We associated a secondary CIDR from the 100.64.0.0/10 carrier-grade NAT range, kept the nodes on the original routable range, and put pods on the secondary range through the CNI's custom networking, which gave pods a huge private pool without burning our scarce routable space. The two senior points I always add are that any peered VPC or Transit Gateway needs its routes updated for the new secondary CIDR, and that the secondary CIDR must still not overlap with anything it connects to — the same non-overlap rule that governs the original plan applies to every block you add later.
